facts.title: Born in a Berkeley Lab
facts.text: Plutonium was first produced in December 1940 and chemically identified in February 1941 by Glenn Seaborg, Edwin McMillan, Joseph Kennedy and Arthur Wahl at the University of California, Berkeley. They made it by bombarding uranium-238 with deuterons in a 60-inch cyclotron, creating neptunium-238 that decayed into plutonium-238. It was the second transuranium element ever discovered, right after neptunium.

facts.title: Named After a Dwarf Planet
facts.text: Following the pattern of uranium (Uranus) and neptunium (Neptune), the new element was named after Pluto, then the outermost planet of the solar system. Seaborg deliberately chose the symbol Pu instead of the more logical Pl, partly as a playful joke that he expected to be rejected but which slipped through unnoticed. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, long after the element's name was set.

facts.title: A Metal That Has Six Forms
facts.text: Solid plutonium is one of the most structurally complex metals known, existing in six distinct crystal phases (allotropes) between room temperature and its melting point of 640 degrees Celsius. These phases have wildly different densities, so a sample can expand or shrink dramatically with small temperature changes. Engineers add a few percent of gallium to stabilize the workable delta phase, a trick essential to fabricating plutonium parts.

facts.title: It Is Warm to the Touch
facts.text: A lump of plutonium-238 feels noticeably warm because its intense alpha radioactivity releases about 0.56 watts of heat per gram. This self-heating is so reliable that the metal can glow a dull red and stay hot for decades without any external power. The property turns a chemical curiosity into a long-lived, compact energy source.

facts.title: Powering Spacecraft for Decades
facts.text: Radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) convert the heat of decaying plutonium-238 directly into electricity using thermocouples, with no moving parts. This technology powers NASA's Voyager 1 and 2 probes (launched 1977 and still transmitting), the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers, and the New Horizons mission to Pluto. With a half-life of about 88 years, Pu-238 keeps instruments running where sunlight is too weak for solar panels.

facts.title: The Engine of Nuclear Reactors
facts.text: Plutonium-239 is fissile, meaning a single neutron can split its nucleus and release more neutrons to sustain a chain reaction. Just a few kilograms can reach critical mass, releasing enormous energy. This is why Pu-239 became central to both nuclear power and weapons, and the bomb dropped on Nagasaki in 1945 used a plutonium core.

facts.title: Almost Absent From Nature
facts.text: Although plutonium is overwhelmingly a man-made element, vanishingly tiny amounts occur naturally. Trace Pu-239 forms in uranium ores when uranium-238 captures stray neutrons from spontaneous fission or cosmic rays. Far larger natural deposits existed about two billion years ago at Oklo in Gabon, where uranium concentrations were high enough to run natural fission reactors that bred plutonium.

facts.title: Forged in Dying Stars
facts.text: Heavy elements like plutonium are created in the cosmos by the rapid neutron-capture process, which requires the violent neutron flux of merging neutron stars and possibly some supernovae. The isotope plutonium-244 has a half-life of about 80 million years, long enough that scientists search deep-sea sediments for traces deposited by ancient nearby explosions. Such measurements help reveal how often these cataclysmic events seeded our region of the galaxy.

facts.title: A Surprising Chemical Chameleon
facts.text: In water, plutonium can simultaneously exist in four different oxidation states, from +3 to +6, each with its own color, ranging from blue-violet to orange. This makes its solution chemistry among the most complex of any element and a genuine headache for engineers reprocessing nuclear fuel. The behavior stems from its 5f electrons, which sit on a knife-edge between being chemically active and locked away.

facts.title: Dangerous Mainly When Inhaled
facts.text: Plutonium emits alpha particles that cannot penetrate skin or even a sheet of paper, so handling sealed sources is far less hazardous than its reputation suggests. The real danger comes if fine particles are inhaled or enter the bloodstream, where the radiation can damage nearby tissue and lodge in bones and the liver. Because of this, plutonium work demands sealed gloveboxes and strict containment rather than thick external shielding.
